subject: physics_2
question_text: What are the limitations of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom?

mark_split.label: It works only for one-electron atoms
No intensities and no fine structure
No Zeeman effect and no Stark effect
It mixes classical orbits with a quantum rule

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. SOURCE DEFECT: the book prints this question's title TWICE in a row — "What are the limitations of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom ? Limitations of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom ?" — it is ONE question and is authored as one card. Physics hand-checked: the book's six numbered limitations are all correct and are kept as points 1 to 6; the seventh point on the list here (that the theory joins a classical circular orbit to a quantum condition with no reason for either) is added because it is the root of the other six.

recall_prompt: List the limitations of Bohr's theory — which atoms it fails for, which spectral details it misses, and what is wrong with the model itself.

steps.label: Only one-electron atoms
lines: 1. Bohr's theory applies only to hydrogen and
to hydrogen-like ions with one electron
(He⁺, Li²⁺). It could not explain the spectra
of atoms with more than one electron, because
it leaves out the repulsion between electrons.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say one-electron atoms only, and give the reason: electron–electron repulsion is left out.
steps.why: The whole derivation balances one Coulomb attraction against one centripetal force. With two or more electrons there is also repulsion between them, and the simple orbit picture no longer closes.
common_mistakes: Saying it fails for hydrogen. Hydrogen is the one case it does explain.
Naming the failure without the reason. The electron–electron repulsion is the reason.

recall.must_convey: That the theory holds only for hydrogen and one-electron ions and fails for multi-electron atoms.
accept: only hydrogen and hydrogen like ions
repulsion between electrons is not included

steps.memory_tip: One electron in the derivation means one electron in the answer.

steps.label: No intensities, no fine structure
lines: 2. It could not explain why some spectral lines
are brighter than others — it gives no relative
intensities.
3. It could not explain the fine structure: each
line is really a group of very close lines.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two separate points — brightness of lines, and each line splitting into close components.
steps.why: Bohr's rule gives the position of each line but says nothing about how strongly a transition occurs, and it has only one quantum number, so it cannot produce closely spaced components.
common_mistakes: Treating intensity and fine structure as one point. They are two.
Confusing fine structure with the Zeeman splitting. Fine structure appears with no field applied.

recall.must_convey: That the theory gives no relative intensities and no fine structure of the lines.
accept: cannot explain intensity of the lines
each line is really several close lines

steps.memory_tip: How bright, and how many close lines — Bohr gives neither.

steps.label: No Zeeman or Stark effect
lines: 4. It could not explain the Zeeman effect — the
splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field.
5. It could not explain the Stark effect — the
splitting of spectral lines in an electric field.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Name both effects and say which field each needs.
steps.why: Both effects split one line into several, so the atom must have several states of the same Bohr energy. A model with a single quantum number n has no such states to split.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two: Zeeman is magnetic, Stark is electric.
Naming the effects without saying what is observed — the splitting of the lines.

recall.must_convey: That it explains neither the Zeeman effect in a magnetic field nor the Stark effect in an electric field.
accept: splitting of spectral lines in a field

steps.memory_tip: Zeeman needs a magnetic field; Stark needs an electric field.

steps.label: The model itself is mixed
lines: 6. It says nothing about the wave nature of the
electron, and it gives no reason why the orbits
must be circular when elliptical orbits are
also possible.
7. It joins a classical circular orbit to a
quantum condition L = nh/2π with no reason for
either — the two parts do not follow from one
theory.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The deepest point: half classical, half quantum, and nothing links the halves.
steps.why: Every earlier limitation follows from this one. de Broglie later supplied the missing wave picture and quantum mechanics replaced the orbit altogether, which is exactly why Bohr's theory is a step and not the final answer.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the list of failures. The last mark is for saying WHY the model is incomplete.
Saying Bohr's theory is wrong. Its energy levels for hydrogen are right; the model behind them is incomplete.

recall.must_convey: That the theory says nothing about the wave nature of the electron and joins a classical orbit to a quantum condition with no justification.
accept: says nothing about the wave nature of the electron
no reason why orbits are circular

steps.memory_tip: Half classical orbit, half quantum rule, with nothing joining the halves.

insider_note: Number the limitations down the page — the marks follow the count, and a paragraph of prose loses them even when every point is there.
